title: Single-atom-based asynchronous photonic interconnect for scalable modular quantum computing
authors: Jérémy Raskop, Nadav Kandel, Yaniv Amichy, Yaron Jarach, Tal Kanonich, Andrei Militaru, Johannes Fink, Barak Dayan
abstract: Scaling quantum computation beyond the capacity of a single quantum processing unit requires quantum interconnects between modular processors. Optical photons are natural carriers for distributing entanglement between these processors. Most loss-resilient protocols use photonic Bell-state measurements based on the linear-optics type-II fusion gate. The resulting entanglement rate scales quadratically with each processor's typically low photon-delivery probability. Here we analyze a memory-assisted quantum interconnect using a near-deterministic, robust photon--atom controlled-$Z$ gate via a single atom trapped in a high-finesse cavity. Detecting and measuring a photon from one processor heralds entanglement between that processor and the atom. This entanglement is preserved while the process repeats with the second processor until the second photon is detected and measured. Reading out the atomic qubit finalizes the entanglement between the processors. As the entanglement is mediated by the atom, the photons from both processors do not need to be indistinguishable, removing a major source of infidelity. Furthermore, by removing the simultaneous photon-arrival requirement, the protocol allows the entanglement rate to scale linearly rather than quadratically with photon-arrival probability over a wide parameter range. We derive entanglement rates under realistic parameters, accounting for decay of the atom's entanglement with the first processor and for decoherence caused by unheralded photon interactions. The nanosecond-scale of the gate and read-out operations leads to orders-of-magnitude entanglement-rate gain over linear optics, removing a key bottleneck in modular quantum computing.
summary: This paper proposes a memory-assisted quantum interconnect using a trapped atom in a cavity to link modular quantum processors. By allowing photons to arrive sequentially rather than simultaneously, the protocol achieves a linear scaling of the entanglement rate, dramatically improving scalability over existing quadratic-scaling methods. This breakthrough removes a major bottleneck for building large-scale quantum computers.
main_problem: Scaling quantum computation requires robust quantum interconnects to distribute entanglement between modular quantum processing units (QPUs).
main_result: The proposed memory-assisted interconnect achieves an entanglement rate scaling linearly ($\propto p$) with photon probability, offering orders-of-magnitude improvement over the quadratic scaling ($\propto p^2$) of conventional linear-optics methods.
method: The method utilizes a memory-assisted Bell-State Measurement (BSM) mediated by a single trapped atom in a cavity, allowing for sequential photon detection rather than simultaneous arrival.
model_or_system: The system involves single trapped neutral atoms (e.g., Rb) coupled to a high-finesse cavity, implementing photon-atom controlled-Z (CZ) gates. The analysis models the rate by accounting for sequential photon interactions and decoherence.
key_observables: Entanglement rate ($\Gamma$), infidelity ($\delta_{tot}$), and the scaling dependence on photon delivery probability ($p$).
important_parameters: Photon delivery probability ($p$), cavity cooperativity ($C$), coherence time ($ ar{T}^*$), and the total infidelity budget ($\delta$).
main_assumptions: The protocol assumes the memory coherence time is long enough to allow for sequential photon arrivals, and the analysis models the total infidelity as a sum of added noise and memory errors.
figures_summary: Figures compare entanglement rate scaling ($\propto p^2$ vs. $\propto p$), illustrate the sequential vs. simultaneous arrival process, and show trade-offs between rate and pump power/noise.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the limitation of quadratic scaling in standard interconnects. It then details the memory-assisted protocol using sequential CZ gates. The latter sections focus on rigorous rate derivations, modeling the total infidelity budget, and optimizing operational parameters based on noise trade-offs.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a core bottleneck in quantum networking by providing a theoretically derived, high-rate protocol that circumvents the quadratic scaling limitations inherent in standard linear-optics entanglement distribution.

figures.caption: Fig 1 Scaling of the entanglement rate. (a) In conventional type-II fusion, quantum processing units A and B must each successfully deliver a photon in the same attempt. If each does so with probability p at attempt rate R, the entanglement rate scales as Rp2. (b) Using a photon–atom controlled-Z gate, a midpoint atomic qubit memory preserves the entanglement established by whichever photon arrives first while the other QPU continues attempting. If the system coherence time allows a sufficiently long waiting window, the same-attempt requirement is removed and the entanglement rate approaches the linear scaling Rp.

Fig 2 Type-II fusion and atomic-qubit-based Bell-state measurements. (a) Linear-optics BSM. Photons from both QPUs must arrive at the interconnect in the same attempt. (b) Memory-assisted atom–cavity BSM. For each photon, the |0p⟩rail bypasses the cavity, while the |1p⟩rail is reflected from it and acquires an atom-state-dependent phase, implementing the controlled-Z gate. A circulator directs the reflected rail to a balanced beam splitter, where it interferes with the bypassed rail. Detection at either output supplies the herald, and the output port identifies the X- basis outcome. Atomic read-out completes the BSM after a photon from each QPU has been detected and measured. Figure 5 summarizes how the entanglement rate of the memory-assisted interconnect depends on N and ˜pR, together with its gain over type-II fusion. Panel (a) shows the entanglement rate normal- ized by the per-QPU herald rate, Γ/(qR). At small N, the infidelity budget permits no additional attempt, so k = 0 and only same-attempt heralds contribute. As additional attempts become admis- sible, the memory-assisted contribution grows and the curves for different ˜p gradually converge. At large N, unheralded photon interactions limit the waiting-window length, and the normalized rate approaches a plateau below the unbounded-window limit.
